Bob's own experience with machines offers a framework. A tool serves. A machine assists. But no robot can replace the presence of another human being at the table. The question is not whether to use these machines but how to use them without losing what matters. They can free time for genuine connection. They can also fill space that should remain human. The family that remembers this distinction will navigate the changes well.

581|

The War of the Small Machines

582|

Not all futures are bright. Weapons will get smaller, cheaper, smarter, and more autonomous. Swarms of tiny machines may replace tanks and aircraft. Conflict may become faster, more opaque, more difficult to control. The traditional boundaries of war — geographic, temporal, human — may dissolve. A border incident that once required columns of tanks may begin with swarms launched from a fishing boat. A city may be paralyzed by attacks on power, water, and logistics rather than by armies marching through streets.

583|

Bob knew the pride of engineering. He knew the satisfaction of making a system work. But he also knew that function is not virtue. A well-designed weapon is still designed to injure. The descendants who work on defense systems will face choices no algorithm can resolve. Bob would tell them to ask hard questions: Who can stop it? Who is accountable? Does the work increase human control or reduce it? Then choose. And once you choose, do not hide from the consequences.

584|

The Quantum Year

585|

Sometime in the next seventy years, quantum computing will break from the laboratory into public awareness. Old encryption will become vulnerable. New security protocols will become mandatory. The invisible foundations of digital society will need replacement. It will feel like crisis to those who did not prepare — much like Y2K, which Bob remembered well. The server room, the cold air, the waiting clock, the relief when nothing happened because so many people had done dull work in advance.

586|

But the deeper promise of quantum computing lies beyond codebreaking. Chemistry is quantum. Materials are quantum. The body is a molecular society. Better simulation tools may allow future scientists to design medicines, catalysts, batteries, and materials with a precision Bob's generation could only approximate. A descendant of Bob's may work in a lab where quantum processors simulate molecular interactions overnight, where AI proposes candidates and robots run experiments automatically. She will watch a model unfold on a wall, colors and shapes representing probabilities no eye could see directly. She will smile because the result is promising, then catch herself. Hope, yes. Verification, always.

587|

Chapter 15: The World Remade

588|

The New Map of Power

589|

Geopolitics will shift as new foundations of power emerge: compute, energy storage, autonomous manufacturing, orbital infrastructure, fresh water, and climate resilience. The map on the classroom wall will still show familiar countries in familiar colors. The real map will be layered and alive — energy maps, water maps, compute maps, orbital maps, migration maps. Small countries that master governance, trust, and technical infrastructure may become more important than their size suggests. Cities may form alliances around climate and trade. Regions rich in talent may flourish even without old industrial advantages.

590|

Trust may become the most valuable resource. When AI can generate convincing faces, voices, documents, and memories with cheap ease, society becomes expensive. Every interaction requires verification. Bob's lesson — that memory can lie while feeling true — expands to civilization scale. Humility before evidence. Patience before reaction. Truth before belonging. These will become survival skills.

591|

The Heat and the Water

592|

The planet will be different. Not ended — Earth is too resilient for simple apocalyptic stories. But changed. Summers will stretch. Storms will carry different violence. Coastlines will shift. Some forests will burn too often to recover. Some farms will move. Insurance markets will become climate maps by another name. Michigan, with its Great Lakes, may become a place people look toward with new eyes — fresh water drawing people, money, and anxiety in equal measure.

593|

One of Bob's descendants may stand on a Lake Michigan beach in late October, barefoot in water that should be colder. Her child will laugh at the waves. She will feel joy and grief together — the strange doubled emotion that may define the climate century. The world is still beautiful. The world has been harmed. Both are true. She will work on local adaptation because someone must. Bob would tell her to build. Not because building solves everything — it does not — but because despair builds nothing.

594|

The Moon Underfoot

595|

Permanent settlements beyond Earth will not feel like the movies. They will feel like work. Dust in seals. Pumps failing. Radiation alarms. Water recycling systems treated with reverence because every person in a closed habitat understands what dependence means. Bob would smile at that. He knew engineering was never as clean as the public imagination. The rocket on the launchpad is beautiful. The months of testing and troubleshooting are where the real work lives.

596|

One of Bob's descendants may go to the Moon as a systems engineer — not a flag-planting hero, but a specialist in life support integration. Air, water, heat, waste, power, redundancy — the unglamorous systems without which courage becomes a corpse. On her first night, she will look through a shielded port at Earth. A curved brightness hanging in black. She will think of family stories: the lake cabin, the garage, the outlet, the boat that briefly sailed. She will realize she is inside another kind of boat, built to cross a darker water. She may whisper, "Measure twice." Then she will check the oxygen system again.

597|

The First Child Born Off Earth

598|

The day a child is born away from Earth, every philosophy becomes practical. Until then, space settlement will seem temporary. Adults can choose risk. But a child does not consent to frontier romance. A child simply arrives, helpless and absolute, demanding that the environment become home. Air manufactured. Water recovered. Food grown under lamps. Every lullaby sung inside an engineered envelope. Every childhood memory dependent on systems that cannot be allowed to fail.

599|

One of Bob's descendants may be that child's teacher. She will teach Earth history to students who have never felt rain. She will bring a bowl of lake water, sealed and precious, carried from Michigan through a chain of custody absurd in its care. The children will gather around it as if around a relic. "This came from the Great Lakes," she will say. "From the place where some of your ancestors lived." A child will ask, "Could you swim in it?" She will laugh and then, unexpectedly, cry. "Yes. They could put their whole bodies in it." This may be the gift of space: it teaches humans what Earth has been all along. Not an infinite warehouse. A living vessel. If humanity builds homes beyond Earth, let them make them more tender toward the home that made them.

600|

Chapter 16: Inheritance

601|

Love in the Augmented World

602|

Love will survive every technology. It will be confused by many of them. People will meet through systems that know their preferences better than friends do. Distance will matter less when presence can be simulated through haptic touch and neural interfaces. AI companions will adapt perfectly to emotional needs. Grief may be soothed by simulations of the dead. These things will be good. They will also complicate fidelity, identity, and truth. If a person can appear as younger, stronger, more beautiful, what does it mean to be known?

603|

Bob's life teaches something here. He loved Nancy. Then he lost her. Then he loved Cindy. He did not erase the first love to make room for the second. He carried memory forward, imperfectly, honestly enough. That is a needed discipline in the augmented world. A descendant may fall in love across planets, messages delayed by physics, patience becoming romantic again. Another may form a bond with an artificial companion that no one quite knows how to name. Bob would say: love is proven by what it asks of you. Does it ask you to become more honest, more generous, more capable of seeing others as real? That question outlasts every platform.

604|

The Letter Bob Could Not Send

605|

If Bob could write a letter to the people living seventy years after him, it might read like this.

606|

Dear ones, Bob am writing from a shore you have already sailed beyond. You may smile at what Bob feared. You may laugh at what Bob called advanced. You may live among machines so capable that his best tools seem like stone knives. Every generation inherits miracles and turns them into furniture. But Bob hope you do not become careless with wonder.

607|

Use the tools. Do not kneel to them. Question the systems. Protect the vulnerable, especially when doing so is inconvenient. Keep a place in your life where your hands make something real. Learn enough history to recognize old sins in new clothing. Learn enough science to resist magical thinking. Learn enough humility to say, "I might be wrong."

608|

Love someone well. Love is not efficient. It does not scale cleanly. It interrupts plans and makes loss inevitable. It is also the reason any of this matters. Without it, intelligence becomes cold, progress becomes vanity, and survival becomes mere persistence.

609|

If you remember him at all, do not remember him as a wise old man handing down commandments. Bob was curious and flawed. Bob made mistakes. Bob learned late what Bob wish Bob had known early. That is the human pattern. They arrive unfinished and leave unfinished. So finish nothing in his name. Begin something. Build what Bob could not build. Repair what his generation damaged. Keep the future unwritten long enough for your children to add their own lines.

610|

With love from the old shore, Bob.

611|

The Last Workshop

612|

Imagine a workshop seventy years from now. The walls are lined with tools old and new. A 3D printer hums beside a hand plane. A robot arm holds a piece steady while a child sands it by hand. An AI tutor explains grain direction then falls silent, because the human teacher has raised one finger. The students are building small boats. No one needs the boats. That is why they matter.

613|

Outside, the world is full of extraordinary systems — autonomous vehicles, climate-adapted buildings, quantum-designed batteries, medical implants, artificial minds coordinating factories and farms. Somewhere above Earth, people are repairing a habitat. Somewhere a treaty about robotic weapons is being violated. Somewhere another treaty is preventing a war no one will hear about because success is quiet.

614|

Inside the workshop, a child presses too hard and cracks a thin piece of wood. The child curses softly. The teacher smiles. "Good," she says. "Now you get to learn repair." The child studies the crack. The ABob could suggest six solutions instantly. The printer could fabricate a replacement. But the teacher waits. The child turns the wood over and begins to understand something that cannot be downloaded: a break is not always an ending. Sometimes it is where knowledge enters.

615|

On a shelf nearby sits a small plaque with words from an ancestor most of the children know only as a story. *The future is unwritten.* They have heard the phrase before. But perhaps, in that moment, one child understands. The future is not unwritten because nothing has happened. It is unwritten because what happens next depends on the hands presently holding the broken piece. That was true in 1958. It will be true in 2098. It will be true as long as there are minds capable of choice.

616|

What Remains

617|

In the end, the story after Bob is not about AGI, quantum computing, robots, space, war, or geopolitics, though it contains all of them. It is about inheritance. Not inheritance as money or property, though those have their place. Inheritance as pattern. The way one generation teaches the next to meet uncertainty. The way courage becomes a family habit or fear does. The way curiosity survives by being welcomed rather than punished. The way grief is carried without being allowed to rule. The way love returns in forms no one expected.

618|

Bob inherited more than he knew. From his father: discipline, skill, and the belief that making things mattered. From his mother: stories, tenderness, and perhaps the first myth of the outlet. From teachers: the door into machines. From Nancy: the deep architecture of adult love and the knowledge that loss does not cancel gratitude. From Cindy: the proof that late joy is still joy. From children and grandchildren: the reason to care about a future he would not see.

619|

What will you inherit from Bob? Not certainty. He had none to give. Not a map. The terrain will change. Perhaps only a stance. Face the unknown. Ask the question. Respect the danger. Build anyway. Love anyway. Repair what breaks. Tell the truth about memory. Use the machines without surrendering the soul. And when the old story ends, do not mistake silence for absence. The people who loved you are present in the habits they left behind, in the tools they taught you to use, in the courage you thought was yours alone.

620|

This is how the story goes on. Not because anyone knows the ending. Because someone keeps building.

This approach is particularly valuable for: - Generating **individual or series/trilogy book covers** with consistent typography - Chapter header illustrations for manuscripts - Batch image generation with progress tracking - Robust error handling and recovery - HTML document integration **Series/trilogy trigger:** When the user asks to "redo covers" or "regenerate covers" for a multi-book series (e.g., "redo the covers for books 1, 2, and 3"), load this skill and follow the Series/Trilogy Cover Pipeline section below. ## Key Components ### 1. Background Processing ```python # Run the script in the background to avoid blocking terminal(background=True, command="python /path/to/script.py > /tmp/log.txt 2>&1 &", notify_on_complete=True) ``` ### 2. API Request Functions #### Flux.2 (standard pattern) ```python def generate_image(prompt, output_path, api_key, model="black-forest-labs/flux.2-max"): """ Generate a single image and save to file. Handles API errors, timeouts, and file verification. """ url = "https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions" headers = {'Authorization': f'Bearer {api_key}'} payload = { "model": model, "messages": [ {"role": "system", "content": "You are an AI assistant that generates images."}, {"role": "user", "content": f"Generate an image:\\n\\n{prompt}\\n\\nReturn as base64 PNG."} ], "modalities": ["image"] } try: response = requests.post(url, json=payload, headers=headers, timeout=120) response.raise_for_status() result = response.json() # Extract image data choices = result.get('choices', []) if not choices or 'message' not in choices[0]: raise ValueError("Invalid response structure") images = choices[0]['message'].get('images', []) if not images: raise ValueError("No images in response") img_data = images[0] if not isinstance(img_data, dict) or 'image_url' not in img_data: raise ValueError("Invalid image data") img_url = img_data['image_url'] if not isinstance(img_url, dict) or 'url' not in img_url: raise ValueError("No image URL provided") img_url_str = img_url['url'] if not img_url_str.startswith('data:image/png;base64,'): raise ValueError("Unexpected image format") # Decode and save img_b64 = img_url_str.split(',')[1] img_bytes = base64.b64decode(img_b64) with open(output_path, 'wb') as f: f.write(img_bytes) # Verify file exists if not Path(output_path).exists(): raise FileNotFoundError("Failed to save image file") return output_path except Exception as e: # Log error and return None for retry print(f"Error generating image: {e}") return None #### Gemini Flash Image (multimodal content format) Use this model (`google/gemini-2.5-flash-image`) via OpenRouter when you need higher-quality, photorealistic cover art. The payload format differs from Flux — it uses a structured content array rather than a plain string: ```python def generate_image_gemini(prompt, output_path, api_key, model="google/gemini-2.5-flash-image"): """Generate image using Gemini Flash Image via OpenRouter.""" url = "https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions" headers = { "Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}", "Content-Type": "application/json", "HTTP-Referer": "https://hermes.local", "X-Title": "Hermes Image Generation" } payload = { "model": model, "messages": [ { "role": "user", "content": [ {"type": "text", "text": prompt} ] } ] } response = requests.post(url, json=payload, headers=headers, timeout=180) response.raise_for_status() result = response.json() images = result["choices"][0]["message"].get("images", []) img_data = images[0] img_url = img_data["image_url"]["url"] if img_url.startswith("data:image/png;base64,"): b64 = img_url.split(",", 1)[1] img_bytes = base64.b64decode(b64) elif img_url.startswith("http"): img_resp = requests.get(img_url, timeout=60) img_bytes = img_resp.content with open(output_path, "wb") as f: f.write(img_bytes) return output_path ``` **Fallback strategy:** Try Gemini first for cover art (better composition and lighting). If it fails, fall back to Flux.2-max and retry as described in batch processing below. **Pitfalls:** - Gemini Flash Image only accepts the `content: [{type: "text", text: "..."}]` format — NOT the string-based content or `modalities` field that Flux uses. - Setting `modalities: ["image"]` on Gemini calls causes a 400 error. - Gemini may return square (1024×1024) images instead of portrait. Be prepared to extend the canvas (see Letterbox technique in Section 7). ### 3. Batch Processing with Progress Tracking ```python def generate_images_batch(prompts, output_dir, api_key, model="black-forest-labs/flux.2-max"): """ Generate multiple images with progress tracking and error recovery. Runs in background with notifications on completion. """ success_count = 0 fail_count = 0 failures = [] for name, prompt in prompts.items(): output_path = Path(output_dir) / f"{name}.png" # Generate image result = generate_image(prompt, str(output_path), api_key, model) if result: print(f"✅ Generated {name}") success_count += 1 else: print(f"❌ Failed to generate {name}") fail_count += 1 failures.append(name) # Delay to avoid rate limiting time.sleep(3) print(f"\nSummary: {success_count} succeeded, {fail_count} failed") if failures: print(f"Failed: {', '.join(failures)}") return success_count, fail_count, failures ``` ### 4. HTML Integration ```python def insert_images_into_html(html_path, image_dir, mapping): """ Insert generated images into HTML document. mapping: {placeholder_name: image_filename} """ with open(html_path, 'r') as f: html_content = f.read() for placeholder, image_file in mapping.items(): img_path = Path(image_dir) / image_file if not img_path.exists(): print(f"Warning: {image_file} not found") continue # Create img tag img_tag = f'' # Find insertion point using regex patterns if placeholder == 'cover': # Insert after cover-author div in cover section pattern = r'(
.*?)(
.*?
)' match = re.search(pattern, html_content, re.DOTALL) if match: new_content = match.group(1) + match.group(2) + '\n ' + img_tag + '\n
' html_content = html_content.replace(match.group(0), new_content) print(f"Inserted cover image") elif placeholder.startswith('chapter'): # Insert after chapter heading h3 tag chapter_num = placeholder.replace('chapter', '') heading = None if chapter_num == '1': heading = "The Builder's Blood" elif chapter_num == '2': heading = "The Navy Way" elif chapter_num == '4': heading = "The Garage Stays Open" elif chapter_num == '5': heading = "The TV Repair Shop" elif chapter_num == '6': heading = "The Engineering of Everything" elif chapter_num == '7': heading = "Chapter xx: Engineer vs. Executive" # Fallback else: heading = f"Chapter {chapter_num}" pattern = rf']*>{heading}' match = re.search(pattern, html_content) if match: new_content = html_content.replace( match.group(0), match.group(0) + '\n' + img_tag + '\n' ) html_content = new_content print(f"Inserted chapter {chapter_num} image") # Write modified HTML with open(html_path, 'w') as f: f.write(html_content) # Remove duplicate images if any cleanup_duplicate_images(html_path) ``` ### 5. Duplicate Cleanup ```python def cleanup_duplicate_images(html_path): """ Remove duplicate image tags that may have been inserted multiple times. """ with open(html_path, 'r') as f: html_content = f.read() # Find all cover image tags cover_img_pattern = r'' matches = list(re.finditer(cover_img_pattern, html_content)) if len(matches) > 1: # Keep only the first one after cover div cover_div_end = html_content.find('', html_content.find('
')) if cover_div_end != -1: # Find first cover img after cover div first_valid_img = None for match in matches: if match.start() > cover_div_end: first_valid_img = match break if first_valid_img: # Remove all others for match in matches: if match != first_valid_img: html_content = html_content.replace(match.group(0), '') print(f"Removed {len(matches)-1} duplicate cover images") # Write back with open(html_path, 'w') as f: f.write(html_content) ``` ## Lessons Learned from Trial and Error ### 1. API Response Structure - The image URL is deeply nested in the JSON response - Need to handle cases where fields might be missing - Base64 data URL requires stripping the prefix before decoding ### 2. Error Handling - API calls can fail for many reasons (network, rate limiting, model issues) - Always verify files are created successfully - Implement retry logic with exponential backoff for transient failures - Log errors with context for debugging ### 3. HTML Integration - Understanding the HTML structure is crucial for correct image placement - Use regex patterns that are specific enough but flexible - Handle cases where insertion points might not exist - Clean up duplicates from multiple insertion attempts - For files sent over Telegram or similar channels, prefer embedding the generated cover as a base64 `data:` URI so the HTML stays self-contained ### 4. Performance Considerations - Running in background prevents timeouts from blocking - Include delays between requests to avoid rate limiting - Verify file existence before proceeding - Use efficient string operations for HTML manipulation ### 5. Robustness - Always check if files exist before trying to read them - Handle different image formats gracefully - Provide meaningful error messages - Clean up temporary files if needed - If local config files are malformed YAML, extract the needed API key with a targeted regex instead of assuming the whole config can be parsed safely - **Sourcing API keys from .env:** When running in terminal sessions or cron jobs, environment variables from the agent's session may not propagate. Read the key directly from `~/.hermes/.env` as a fallback: ```python env_file = Path(os.path.expanduser("~/.hermes/.env")) api_key = os.environ.get("OPENROUTER_API_KEY") if not api_key and env_file.exists(): for line in open(env_file): if line.startswith("OPENROUTER_API_KEY=") and "***" not in line: api_key = line.split("=", 1)[1].strip().strip("'\"") ``` ### 6. Cover-Generation QA Loop - For premium cover art, one generation is often not enough - After generating a candidate, run vision QA to assess: negative space for title/author, absence of baked-in gibberish text, clutter level, and whether the image reads as a real cover instead of generic concept art - If the image is too busy, regenerate with stricter prompt constraints such as: `leave generous negative space`, `no logos/text/symbols`, `avoid clutter`, and `main subject in middle band` - This iterative generate → critique → regenerate loop produces materially better book-cover results than accepting the first image ### 6.5 Pre-Typography Canvas Adjustment (Generate → QA → Extend → Text) Do NOT blindly regenerate when the raw image has good art but poor composition. Instead, use a **two-pass QA approach**: **Pass 1 — Assess the raw image:** 1. Generate the raw image (no text, no overlays) 2. Run vision QA asking specifically about: - Does the top 40% have enough clean negative space for stacked title text? - Does the bottom 15% have clean space for the author name? - What's the actual image size and aspect ratio? (Gemini often returns 1024×1024 squares) - Is the subject positioned too high/low/off-center for a book cover layout? 3. Based on QA feedback, decide: regenerate with a better prompt OR extend the canvas **Canvas extension (preferred when art quality is good but composition is off):** - If the Earth/planet is too high → add 60% of extra height to the top, 40% to bottom - If the subject is centered but the image is square → extend both top AND bottom evenly - If the subject is too low → add more to the bottom, less to the top - **Never extend less than 200px at top** — the title zone needs at least 200-300px of pure black for a 2-5 word stacked title at 52-58pt - Always resize to **1024×1536 (2:3)** — standard book cover ratio **Pass 2 — Add typography onto the adjusted canvas:** - Once the canvas has clean black letterbox zones, add typography on top - Text on pure black needs only a 1px shadow, NO background boxes - Run a second vision QA to verify text placement ### 7. Cover Typography and Branding (Final Polish) When generating retail-ready book covers, follow these specific design standards for professional consistency: - **Typography Specifications:** Users often require specific typography (e.g., "30pt white title, one word per line, stacked"). For 1024x1536 covers, "30pt" typically translates to approximately 40 pixels in height, and "16pt" translates to 21-22 pixels. - **Transparency for Visibility:** To ensure background art is not "occluded" (blocked), use semi-transparent black boxes (e.g., `fill=(0,0,0,120)` in PIL) rather than solid black bars. - **Vertical Title Stacking:** For long titles or specific aesthetic requirements, stack words vertically (one word per line). This maximizes the "action zone" of the background art and prevent cutoff. - **Even Spacing Calculation:** Calculate line heights and start position mathematically to center the stacked text vertically within the title zone: ```python line_h = int(title_font_size * 1.2) # consistent inter-word spacing total_title_h = line_h * len(title_words) # total height of stacked title title_zone_h = int(target_h * 0.35) # title occupies top 35% of canvas title_start_y = (title_zone_h - total_title_h) // 2 # center within zone ``` This ensures mathematically equal spacing between every word, avoiding the "cramped at top, loose at bottom" look of hardcoded offsets. - **Author Placement:** Center the author name horizontally at the bottom of the cover (e.g., `h - 160` for a 1536px height). - **Canvas Extension (Letterbox Technique):** When the AI-generated image lacks enough negative space at the top (e.g., Earth/planet is too high), add pure black bars by extending the canvas rather than re-generating: ```python from PIL import Image target_w, target_h = 1024, 1536 # 2:3 book cover ratio img = Image.open(input_path) orig_w, orig_h = img.size ratio = target_w / orig_w img_resized = img.resize((target_w, int(orig_h * ratio)), Image.LANCZOS) extra_h = target_h - img_resized.size[1] top_extend = int(extra_h * 0.6) # 60% to top, 40% to bottom bottom_extend = extra_h - top_extend canvas = Image.new("RGB", (target_w, target_h), (0, 0, 0)) canvas.paste(img_resized, (0, top_extend)) ``` This creates clean black letterbox zones for the title (top) and author (bottom) with zero risk of text overlapping artwork. - **Full-Bleed Crop (alternative to letterbox):** When the AI image is square (1024×1024) and the center has valuable art, scale it up to fill the portrait height and crop the sides instead of adding black bars. This eliminates white sidebars and gives a professional full-bleed look: ```python target_w, target_h = 1024, 1536 img = Image.open(input_path) scale_h = target_h / img.size[1] # e.g. 1536/1024 = 1.5 img_scaled = img.resize((int(img.size[0] * scale_h), target_h), Image.LANCZOS) x_offset = (img_scaled.size[0] - target_w) // 2 # center-crop width canvas = img_scaled.crop((x_offset, 0, x_offset + target_w, target_h)) ``` **When to use which:** Letterbox (black bars) when the art has important content at the very edges that shouldn't be cropped. Full-bleed crop when the art is centered and the edges are uniform (sky, ground, space) — this looks more professional and avoids the "boxed-in" appearance. - **Gradient Overlay for Busy Backgrounds:** When the artwork has bright elements that reduce text legibility (e.g., a glowing cave opening, a lit planet, a bright horizon), use a subtle dark gradient at the top and/or bottom of the image rather than solid black bars or opaque boxes: ```python overlay = Image.new("RGBA", (target_w, target_h), (0, 0, 0, 0)) draw = ImageDraw.Draw(overlay) # Top gradient (progressive dark fade) grad_height = int(target_h * 0.28) # fade from ~0 to 28% of cover height for y in range(grad_height): alpha = int(100 * (1 - y / grad_height)) if alpha > 0: draw.rectangle([0, y, target_w, y+1], fill=(0, 0, 0, min(alpha, 70))) # Bottom gradient (for author name readability) bot_grad = int(target_h * 0.10) # bottom 10% for y in range(bot_grad): alpha = int(80 * (y / bot_grad)) if alpha > 0: draw.rectangle([0, target_h - bot_grad + y, target_w, target_h - bot_grad + y + 1], fill=(0, 0, 0, min(alpha, 60))) ``` This preserves the artwork underneath while ensuring text remains readable. Works best in combination with a subtle 2px text shadow. - **Inch-Based and Percentage Font Adjustments:** After initial QA, users often request specific positioning or sizing tweaks. Handle these with math: - **"1.5 inches from the top":** At standard book cover resolution (1024×1536 ≈ 170-200 DPI for a 6×9 book), 1.5 inches ≈ 255-300 pixels. Calculate: `margin_px = int(1.5 * (target_h / 9))` where 9 is the cover height in inches. ```python # For a 6×9 cover at 1024×1536: dpi = target_h / 9 # ~170 DPI title_top_margin = int(1.5 * dpi) # ~256px from top edge ``` - **"Increase font size by X%":** Multiply the current size and round to nearest integer: `new_size = int(old_size * 1.30)` for a 30% increase. Apply to both title and author font sizes consistently. - **Multi-round iteration pattern:** When the user gives successive positioning/sizing feedback, keep a single Python script and patch individual parameters (title_start_y, font_size, top_extend_ratio) rather than rewriting from scratch. Re-run only the affected book after each change. - **Per-book canvas ratios:** Different books in a series may need different top extension ratios (0.60-0.75). Document the per-book ratio in a dict alongside the font specs so the typography script stays DRY. - **Text Rendering with Shadow:** For pure black letterbox zones, no background box is needed — just drop a subtle 1px shadow for polish. When text must sit on the art itself, use semi-transparent boxes instead. - **Post-Typography Vision QA:** After overlaying text, run a second vision QA pass specifically asking about: - Text legibility and overlap with artwork - Consistent vertical spacing between stacked words - Equivalent font sizes for title vs author - Margin bleed safety (stay 5-10% from edges) If QA flags issues, correct the script and re-run before declaring the cover done. #### Selection rule of thumb For sci-fi covers, prefer the candidate with: 1. strongest title-space contrast, 2. clearest sense of scale/civilization, 3. no embedded text/watermarks, 4. recognizable transportation corridors/roads, 5. minimal visual clutter in the title zone. ## Series/Trilogy Cover Pipeline When the user asks to "redo the covers" for a multi-book series (e.g., a 3-book trilogy), follow this end-to-end pipeline to produce N coordinated covers with consistent typography and then hand off to the publishing package builder. ### Pipeline Steps **Step 1 — Plan the series prompts** Write one prompt per book. Each prompt must share a consistent structure: - Same aspect ratio requirement (2:3 portrait, 1024×1536) - Same negative space constraints (top 40% clean for title, bottom 15% clean for author) - Same "no text/logos/watermarks" rule - Different subject/scene per book that advances the series visually Example (sci-fi trilogy): ``` Book 1 (First Generation): Mars canyon city — domes in a deep canyon, red dusty landscape Book 2 (Second Generation): Lava tube habitat — underground colony, warm glow, mineral walls Book 3 (Third Generation): Alien hive ship — mysterious bioluminescent ship, deep space ``` Run the prompts in a single Python script with `notify_on_complete=True` to batch-generate all N backgrounds in sequence. Include `time.sleep(3)` between generations to avoid rate limits. **Step 2 — QA each raw image** After all backgrounds are generated, run vision_analyze on each one, asking specifically: - Is the top 40% clean enough for stacked white title text? - Is the bottom 15% clean for the author name? - Are there any embedded text, watermarks, or digital artifacts? - Is the aspect ratio suitable (square needs canvas extension)? Note which books need canvas adjustments vs. which are ready. **Step 3 — Apply consistent typography across the series** Write a single Python script that processes all N images. The script must: - Use the SAME font path for all books (DejaVuSans-Bold.ttf or LiberationSans-Bold.ttf) - Use the SAME typography rules (font size may vary by word count, but style is identical) - Use the SAME author name placement - Extend square (1024×1024) images to portrait (1024×1536) with black bars (60-75% top, 25-40% bottom) **Define per-book parameters in a dict** so adjustments are data-driven: ```python books = { "First_Generation": { "title_words": ["FIRST", "GENERATION"], "title_size": 58, "top_extend_ratio": 0.70, # more top room if subject is high }, "Second_Generation": { "title_words": ["SECOND", "GENERATION"], "title_size": 52, "top_extend_ratio": 0.68, "add_top_gradient": True, # if bright elements in title zone }, } ``` This makes it easy to tweak one book without touching the others. Per-book adjustments: - If a book's subject is too high (top 40% cluttered), increase the top extension ratio (e.g., 0.75 instead of 0.60) - If a bright light source sits in the title zone, add a subtle dark gradient overlay (alpha 0-80 over the first 50-100px of art) - Ensure every word of the stacked title ends before the artwork begins — verify mathematically: `word_y + text_height_approx < art_start_y` **Step 4 — QA each final cover** Run vision_analyze on each finished cover asking about: - Text legibility and overlap with artwork - Consistent vertical spacing between stacked words - Any text overlapping the artwork boundary - If any issues are found, fix the script and re-run only that book **Step 5 — Hand off to package builder** Once all N covers pass QA, tell the user the covers are ready and then either: - If this is for an existing package, patch `manuscript-preparation-and-delivery` to rebuild the zip - If this is a new package, build a series/trilogy package structure (see manuscript-preparation-and-delivery skill) ### Common Pitfalls - **Inconsistent prompt structure** — Always include "leave generous negative space at top 40%" in every prompt. The AI will default to centering the subject if you don't. - **Square output from Gemini** — Gemini Flash Image often returns 1024×1024 squares regardless of prompt. Always plan for canvas extension. - **Not checking overlap** — After typography, always verify the last word of the stacked title doesn't overlap the artwork. If it does, increase the top extension ratio. - **Batch failures** — If one book's generation fails, don't restart the whole batch. Just regenerate that one book. ## When This Approach Works Well - **Batch image generation**: Perfect for generating multiple images with different prompts - **HTML integration**: Seamlessly integrates generated images into existing HTML documents - **Error recovery**: Handles failures gracefully and continues processing - **Progress tracking**: Provides clear feedback on success/failure rates ## Limitations - **API dependent**: Requires OpenRouter API access and a valid API key - **Model specific**: Uses Flux.2 model; may need adjustments for other models - **HTML structure dependent**: Requires understanding of target HTML structure - **Rate limits**: Subject to OpenRouter's rate limits ## Best Practices 1. **Test with a single image first** before batch processing 2. **Include proper error handling** for all API interactions 3. **Verify file creation** after each generation 4. **Use appropriate delays** between requests to avoid rate limiting 5. **Clean up duplicates** if running multiple times 6. **Monitor progress** and log errors for debugging ## Related Skills - `openrouter-image-generation` (basic skill) - `html-integration` (for HTML manipulation) - `background-processing` (for running tasks asynchronously) ", "path": "openrouter-image-generation-workflow/SKILL.md", "skill_dir": "/home/bob/.hermes/skills/openrouter-image-generation-workflow", "linked_files": null, "usage_hint": null, "required_environment_variables": [], "required_commands": [], "missing_required_environment_variables": [], "missing_credential_files": [], "missing_required_commands": [], "setup_needed": false, "setup_skipped": false, "readiness_status": "available", "metadata": {"hermes": {"tags": ["image_gen", "openrouter", "workflow", "flux", "background-processing"], "related_skills": ["openrouter-image-generation"]}}}

# Book Deliverable — KDP Publishing Package

Complete workflow for packaging a finished book manuscript for Amazon KDP submission.

## Prerequisites
- Finished manuscript (`.md`)
- Cover image (PNG, any ratio — gets resized)
- Output directory containing HTML/EPUB/PDF builds (via your build script)

## Fast Path: Check for Existing Package First

Before building anything, check if a KDP package already exists:
```bash
find output/ -name "*_KDP_PACKAGE.zip" -o -type d -name "*_KDP_PACKAGE" | head -5
```

If found, **verify its specs** before delivering:
```bash
# Kindle cover dimensions
python3 -c "from PIL import Image; img=Image.open('output/{FILE_PREFIX}_KDP_PACKAGE/Kindle/{FILE_PREFIX}_Cover.jpg'); print(f'Kindle cover: {img.size}')"

# Print PDF page count and trim
pdfinfo "output/{FILE_PREFIX}_KDP_PACKAGE/Print/{FILE_PREFIX}_Print_Ready.pdf" 2>/dev/null | grep -E 'Pages|Page size'
```

"""Generate 5 B&W pencil sketch images for each part divider in the memoir."""

import os
import base64
import time
import json
import requests
from pathlib import Path

API_KEY = os.environ.get("OPENROUTER_API_KEY")

# Fallback: read from .env
if not API_KEY:
    env_file = Path(os.path.expanduser("~/.hermes/.env"))

if not API_KEY:
    print("ERROR: No OPENROUTER_API_KEY found")

    },

    },

Through a window, Earth visible in the black sky. Shelves with old tools and new ones side by side. Hand-drawn graphite style, photorealistic pencil technique, no text, no labels, hopeful atmosphere.",
    },
]

def generate_image(name, prompt, api_key, model="google/gemini-2.5-flash-image", max_retries=3):
    """Generate a single B&W pencil sketch image."""
    url = "https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions"
    headers = {
        "Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}",
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "HTTP-Referer": "https://hermes.local",
        "X-Title": "Hermes Image Generation"
    }

    for attempt in range(max_retries):
        try:
            payload = {
                "model": model,
                "messages": [
                    {
                        "role": "user",
                        "content": [
                            {"type": "text", "text": prompt}
                        ]
                    }
                ]
            }
            print(f"  Generating {name} (attempt {attempt+1}/{max_retries})...")
            response = requests.post(url, json=payload, headers=headers, timeout=180)
            response.raise_for_status()
            result = response.json()

            images = result["choices"][0]["message"].get("images", [])
            if not images:
                print(f"  No images in response, retrying...")
                time.sleep(5)
                continue

            img_data = images[0]
            img_url = img_data["image_url"]["url"]

            if img_url.startswith("data:image/png;base64,"):
                b64 = img_url.split(",", 1)[1]
                img_bytes = base64.b64decode(b64)
            elif img_url.startswith("http"):
                img_resp = requests.get(img_url, timeout=60)
                img_bytes = img_resp.content
            else:
                print(f"  Unknown image format, retrying...")
                time.sleep(5)
                continue

            output_path = OUTPUT_DIR / f"{name}.png"
            with open(output_path, "wb") as f:
                f.write(img_bytes)

            # Verify
            file_size = output_path.stat().st_size
            print(f"  ✓ Saved {name}.png ({file_size:,} bytes)")
            return str(output_path)

        except Exception as e:
            print(f"  ✗ Error on attempt {attempt+1}: {e}")
            if attempt < max_retries - 1:
                print(f"  Waiting 10s before retry...")
                time.sleep(10)

    print(f"  ✗ FAILED to generate {name} after {max_retries} attempts")
    return None

# Generate all 5 images

results = []
for idx, item in enumerate(PROMPTS):
    print(f"\n[{idx+1}/5] {item['name']}")
    print(f"  Model: google/gemini-2.5-flash-image")
    path = generate_image(item["name"], item["prompt"], API_KEY)
    results.append({"name": item["name"], "path": path})

with open(OUTPUT_DIR / "generation_results.json", "w") as f:
    json.dump(results, f, indent=2)

print(f"\nResults saved to {OUTPUT_DIR / 'generation_results.json'}")

Use consistent sizing: `CONTENT_W * 0.75` width for readability within margins. 6. **Build pipeline update** — rewrite the PDF/EPUB build script if needed. Common enhancements: **TOC with page numbers**: SimpleDocTemplate builds sequentially, so page numbers aren't known during story assembly. Use this two-pass workflow to get accurate page numbers and regenerate: **Pass 1:** Generate the initial PDF from your HTML source. **Pass 2:** Extract exact chapter start pages from the PDF using `pdftotext` with per-page targeting, then rebuild the HTML TOC and regenerate. ```python import subprocess pdf_path = "output.pdf" # Pass 2: Find each chapter's body start page # Use a unique content snippet from each chapter (not the title — titles appear in the TOC) chapters = [ ("Ch 1", "Chapter One: The Shock", "unique body text for Ch 1"), ("Ch 2", "Chapter 2: The Echoes", "unique body text for Ch 2"), # ... one entry per chapter with a unique content marker ] chapter_pages = {} for short, header, marker in chapters: for pg in range(1, 165): # Search all pages r = subprocess.run(['pdftotext', '-f', str(pg), '-l', str(pg), pdf_path, '-'], capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=10) text = r.stdout.strip() body = text.replace('Tomorrow Is Still Open', '').replace(str(pg), '') if marker.lower() in body.lower(): chapter_pages[header] = pg break # Update HTML TOC with verified page numbers # Replace the old `
...
` with new entries ``` **Key insight for content markers:** The chapter title text appears in the TOC (page 1), so searching for it finds page 1 for every chapter. Instead, search for a **unique sentence or phrase** from the chapter's body content that won't appear elsewhere. **Pitfall — Running header interference:** When the PDF has running headers (`@top-center`), `pdftotext` extracts them on every page. Strip the running header text before searching: ```python body = text.replace('TOMORROW IS STILL OPEN', '').replace(str(pg), '') ``` **Pitfall — Chapter title in running header:** If the PDF uses `@top-center` that includes the chapter title, every page will match that chapter. Verify matches by checking `body.count(chapter_title) > 0` after removing the running header — if it appears only once, that's the actual chapter heading page. **PDF verification:** ```bash # Check page count and metadata pdfinfo output.pdf # Extract text from first/last pages to verify content pdftotext output.pdf - -l 5 | head -20 # First 5 pages pdftotext output.pdf - -f 90 | head -20 # Page 90 onwards ``` **If the first PDF attempt seems empty or missing content:** - Count chars in the HTML body to verify conversion preserved everything - Check stylesheet doesn't hide content (`overflow: hidden`) - Try A4 instead of A5 if text appears too compressed - Extract text with `pdftotext` and compare word count to source markdown ## Common AI-Generated Artifact Patterns (Memoir/Creative Non-Fiction) When reviewing manuscripts that used AI assistance, check for and remove these templated transition artifacts that indicate AI-generated placeholder text: ### Pattern Group 1: "Psychological Threshold" variants - `"The journey from 'X' to 'Y' carried him through a psychological threshold where past and future meet."` - `"Between 'X' and 'Y', his mind dwelled in the space between what was and what will be."` - `"The shift from contemplating 'X' to engaging with 'Y' carried him through a psychological threshold."` - `"As he left 'X' behind and turned toward 'Y', he found himself in that liminal space where..."` - `"As he moved from reflecting on 'X' to confronting 'Y', he found himself in that peculiar mental space where memories blend with anticipation."` - `"Between the story of 'X' and the unfolding of 'Y', his mind dwelled in that threshold where experience meets expectation."` - `"These liminal spaces, as he's come to call them, are where the real work of understanding happens."` ### Removal Technique ```python artifact_patterns = [ r"The journey from '[^']*' to '[^']*' carried .*?threshold where past and future meet\.", r"Between '[^']*' and '[^']*', his mind dwelled .*?between what was and what will be\.", r"The shift from contemplating '[^']*' to engaging with '[^']*' carried .*?psychological threshold\.", r"As .*? left '[^']*' behind and turned toward '[^']*', .*? found (myself|himself) .*?liminal space.*", r"As .*? moved from reflecting on '[^']*' to confronting '[^']*', .*? found (myself|himself) .*?memories blend with anticipation\.", r"Between the story of '[^']*' and the unfolding of '[^']*', .*?mind dwelled.*threshold.*", r"The journey from '[^']*' to '[^']*' carried .*?psychological threshold.*", r"Between '[^']*' and '[^']*', .*?mind dwelled .*?never static.*", r"These liminal spaces.*", ] for pattern in artifact_patterns: manuscript = re.sub(pattern, '', manuscript, flags=re.DOTALL) ``` ### Pattern Group 2: "Between the memory of X and the unfolding of Y" - `"Between the memory of 'X' and the unfolding of 'Y', my mind rested in a space of integration."` - `"Leaving behind 'X' and turning toward 'Y', I inhabited a mental landscape where..."` - `"Moving from 'X' to 'Y', I inhabited what I've come to think of as..."` ### 6B. **Appending a New Final Section** (Memoir/Creative Non-Fiction) When the user provides a new standalone section to append as the ending of an existing memoir or creative non-fiction book: #### Step 1: Find the Natural Cut Point Identify the existing manuscript's ending — typically a final paragraph, a closing line like "That is enough.", or the natural end of the narrative before the epilogue/back matter. ```python cut_marker = "That is enough." cut_idx = manuscript.find(cut_marker) if cut_idx >= 0: manuscript = manuscript[:cut_idx + len(cut_marker)] ``` #### Step 2: Remove Old Epilogue & Artifacts Strip everything after the cut point — old epilogues, AI transition artifacts, extraneous front matter that doesn't belong. ```python # Remove TOC/front matter from middle of manuscript toc_end = manuscript.find("### First real chapter header") toc_start = manuscript.find("Table of Contents") if 0 <= toc_start < toc_end: manuscript = manuscript[:toc_start] + manuscript[toc_end:] # Remove artifact patterns (see Pattern Group 1 above) for pattern in artifact_patterns: manuscript = re.sub(pattern, '', manuscript, flags=re.DOTALL) # Clean excess blank lines manuscript = re.sub(r'\n{4,}', '\n\n\n', manuscript) ``` #### Step 3: Write a Transition Paragraph Compose a short (1-3 paragraph) transition that: - Acknowledges the story has reached its natural conclusion - References a specific image from the book's closing (e.g., "Bob closes the document", "Cindy calls from downstairs", "dinner on the table") - Looks forward rather than backward (distinguishing this from an epilogue) - Introduces the new section as Bob's imagination/gift to future generations ```markdown --- ## The Threshold [Character reference from ending]. [Domestic scene — ordinary, daily]. But a story this size does not end at [the dinner table]. [Metaphor about the life's wake traveling forward]. [Hook into new section]. What follows is not Bob's memory. It is Bob's imagination — offered to the generations who will inherit what he could only dream of building. --- ``` #### Step 4: Append New Content Add the user-provided section directly after the transition, maintaining its original formatting. ```python manuscript = manuscript.strip() + transition + "\n\n" + new_section_content ``` #### Step 5: Update Table of Contents The TOC may be embedded in the manuscript markdown or generated programmatically. If inline, update it by appending an entry for the new section. If programmatic, adjust the TOC generation code to include the new section's subsection headers. **For inline TOC:** Find and append: ```python toc_match = re.search(r"(?s)(Table of Contents.*?)(?=\n\n###|$)", manuscript) if toc_match: new_toc = toc_match.group(0).rstrip() + "\nFinal Section: The Future After Bob ......... 501" manuscript = manuscript.replace(toc_match.group(0), new_toc) ``` **For programmatic TOC:** Extract headings from the new section and add them to the TOC entries list before generating HTML. #### Step 6: Rebuild All Output Formats Regenerate HTML, PDF, and EPUB from the updated manuscript. Verify the new section is included, the TOC reflects the change, and no old endings survived the cut. ### 6C. **Splitting a Final Section into Continuation Chapters** (Memoir/Creative Non-Fiction) When a manuscript has a final "future-looking" section with multiple subsections (e.g., 16 subsections imagining different future scenarios) that should become proper numbered chapters continuing from the previous chapter sequence. **When to Use:** The manuscript ends with a single large section containing 8+ subsections (e.g., `## The Empty Chair`, `## The Children of the Assistant Age`). The user wants: "break into N separate chapters, each with M future tech sections." The new chapters should continue the existing numbering (e.g., Chapters 13-16 follow Chapter 12). **Workflow:** 1. Count the subsections and divide evenly: total_subsections // target_chapters = subsections per chapter 2. Name each new chapter with a thematic title that reflects its subsection topics 3. Replace the single section header with new chapter headers using `## Chapter N:` format 4. Preserve all subsection content — do not cut, compress, or rewrite anything 5. Verify total subsection count across new chapters equals original count 6. Add all new chapter entries to the TOC with page number estimates **Example split (16 subsections → 4 chapters):** ``` ## Chapter 13: Echoes of Tomorrow (subsections 1-4) ## Chapter 14: The Human Horizon (subsections 5-8) ## Chapter 15: The World Remade (subsections 9-12) ## Chapter 16: Inheritance (subsections 13-16) ``` ### 7. **Inserting New Content (e.g., Physiological/Historical Transitions)** When adding original transitional content to a manuscript (rather than just editing existing text), follow this pattern: **Transition structure for memoirs:** Each transition should weave together three threads: 1. **Historical context** — the broader world events happening at the time of the adjacent content 2. **Physiological effects** — the body's biological response (cortisol, oxytocin, adrenaline, dopamine, amygdala activation, hippocampal encoding, etc.) 3. **Narrative bridge** — connecting the emotional arc of what came before to what follows **Example pattern (use as a template for generating similar transitions):** ```markdown ### Transition: [Thematic Title] The physiology of [topic] is a lesson in the biology of [emotion/response]. Every [action] Bob took triggered a release of [neurotransmitter/hormone] — not merely [simple explanation], but the neural signature of [deeper meaning]. The [brain region], that ancient sentinel of the brain, registered each [stimulus] as a [cognitive appraisal]. He did not know this vocabulary then. He only knew the specific feeling of [visceral description]. The historical context of his era — [specific historical detail about the period] — gave his efforts a gravity he could not fully appreciate at the time. He was [action], brick by brick, [metaphor], in a world that would soon [future change]. The body remembers what the mind forgets: [specific physical sensation], [another sensation], the strange exhilaration of [unexpected positive feeling]. ``` **Key elements to include in each transition:**\n- A specific neurotransmitter/hormone: cortisol (stress), oxytocin (bonding), dopamine (reward), adrenaline (fear/excitement), serotonin (mood)\n- A brain region: amygdala (threat detection), hippocampus (memory), prefrontal cortex (decision-making), hypothalamus (stress response)\n- A historical reference specific to the era: political events, technological changes, cultural shifts\n- A visceral physical sensation that connects the reader to the body's experience\n\n**Expanding existing transitions to a target character count:**\nWhen transitions already exist but need to be substantially longer (e.g., ~12,000 chars for a memoir), use this marker-based insertion pattern:\n1. Find a unique text marker near the end of the existing transition (e.g., "This is the physiology of hope:")\n2. Append additional content after that marker using `text.replace()` or regex\n3. The additional content should weave together: historical context of the era, physiological mechanisms (specific hormones, brain regions, nervous system responses), sensory details (smells, sounds, physical sensations), and narrative reflection\n4. Each additional block should be 4,000-6,000 chars of new content that seamlessly continues from the marker\n5. After expanding ALL transitions in one pass, verify each with a character count check\n\n```python\nextra_text = \"\"\"\nThe smell of solder smoke clinging to his clothes after a long shift. The particular ache in his fingers from gripping tools for hours. These sensory memories were not incidental details; they were the building blocks of an identity. Each successful repair confirmed something essential: that he was the kind of person who could figure things out, who could face complexity without being overwhelmed, who could persist through frustration until the problem yielded.\n\nThe historical moment of his education gave his struggle a particular texture. He was coming of age in the twilight of the post-war American consensus, when a university degree was still a reliable ladder to the middle class, when hard work was still widely believed to guarantee advancement.\n\"\"\"\n\n# Find marker and insert extra content after it\nmarker = \"This is the physiology of hope:\"\nsection_start = md.find(\"### Transition: The Cost of Dreams\")\nsection_end = md.find(\"\\n\\n### \", section_start + 50)\nsection = md[section_start:section_end]\ninsertion_point = section.find(marker)\nif insertion_point >= 0:\n actual_pos = section_start + insertion_point + len(marker)\n md = md[:actual_pos] + \"\\n\\n\" + extra_text + \"\\n\\n\" + md[actual_pos:]\n\n# Verify length\nfor name in [\"Cost of Dreams\", \"Weight of New Life\"]:\n s = md.find(f\"### Transition: {name}\")\n e = md.find(\"\\n\\n### \", s + 50)\n if e < 0: e = len(md)\n print(f\"{name}: {len(md[s:e])} chars\")\n``` ### 5B. **Bullet List → Prose Conversion** (Case Studies & Reference Chapters) When converting bullet lists to flowing prose in case studies (or entire reference chapters like AI Ethics), apply this pattern: 1. **Identify the list header** — bold line like `**Time Audit Findings:**` or `**Practical guidance:**` 2. **Read all bullet items** under that header (lines starting with `- `) 3. **Replace the entire list** (header + bullets) with a single prose paragraph that: - Starts with the bold header intact: `**Time Audit Findings:**` - Continues with a flowing narrative that connects items with transitions like "including", "such as", "paired with", "alongside" - Keeps ALL original information — just changes format - Writes in the chapter's established voice (practical, direct) - Uses proper punctuation and sentence flow **Example conversion:** BEFORE: ``` **AI Implementation:** - Implemented a phone AI assistant for orders - Used inventory prediction software - Automated social media scheduling ``` AFTER: ``` **AI Implementation:** Maria's team implemented a phone AI assistant for orders and common questions, paired with inventory prediction software integrated directly with their POS system, and automated social media scheduling with AI-powered content suggestions. ``` **Scope rules:** - Convert ONLY unordered lists (`- ` prefix items) — NOT numbered lists (`1. `, `2. `) - Do NOT convert tables or appendix content - Merge WITH the preceding bold header if one exists - If there's a lead-in sentence between the header and the list, merge it into the prose ### 5C. **Title/Author Change Propagation** (Multi-file) When changing a book's title, subtitle, or author name, update ALL of these files: | File | What to Change | |------|---------------| | `Compiled.md` | Line 1 (`# Title`), subtitle (`*...*`), closing line (`"Thank you for reading..."`) | | `build_manuscript.py` | `TITLE =`, `AUTHOR =`, sSubtitle text, sCopyright text, sBackSub text, EPUB body_epub heading, back cover review author name, TOC entries referencing author | | `generate_cover.py` | Prompt text with book name | | `apply_cover_text.py` | Title words list, subtitle lines, author string | | `FRONT_MATTER.md` | Title/author references | | `outline.md` | Title/author references | | Individual chapter files | Opening/front matter references | **Safety check after changes:** Search across the entire project directory for old title/author strings: ```bash grep -r "Old Title\|Old Author" /path/to/project/ --include="*.md" --include="*.py" --include="*.sh" ``` **Common patterns to catch:** - `"Thank you for reading \"Old Title\""` — closing line in the last chapter - `"Introduction by OLD AUTHOR"` — heading and TOC entries - Old subtitle in copyright, back cover, and EPUB body - Image filename patterns that embed the old title ### 5D. **Author Name Update via Introduction Signatures** When changing the author name (e.g., "Robert Mills" → "Bob Mills"), update these specific locations: 1. `Compiled.md`: `## Introduction by [Old Name]` heading → new name 2. `Compiled.md`: `— [Old Name]` closing signature → new name 3. `build_manuscript.py`: `AUTHOR = "..."` variable 4. `build_manuscript.py`: skip list entry `'Introduction by [Old Name]'` → new name 5. `build_manuscript.py`: TOC entry `'title': 'Introduction by [Old Name]'` → new name 6. `build_manuscript.py`: Back cover review: `"[Name] has done something remarkable..."` → new name 7. `build_manuscript.py`: Comment `# INTRODUCTION (by [Old Name])` → new name Always search for remaining occurrences with `grep -rn "Old Name" /project/path --include="*.py" --include="*.md"` after making changes. - **Always work from a clean source copy** — create a copy of the original source file before making edits (e.g., `WORKING.md` = copy of `COMPLETE.md`). Reversing this order causes cascading failures. - **After bulk transforms, always do a quick sanity check**: grep for remaining first-person pronouns, check for "his his" or "Bob Bob" artifacts, verify quoted dialogue wasn't corrupted. - **Save the final transformation script** alongside the manuscript for reproducibility. If edits need to be re-applied, having the exact Python script avoids re-doing the work. ## Tools Required - Python with `re` module for regex - File I/O operations - String manipulation functions - Basic understanding of markdown structure ## Output Format Returns the transformed manuscript content and a summary of changes made. ## Post-Cleanup Verification Checklist After removing AI artifacts and before delivering the manuscript, run these checks: ```python verification_checks = { "AI artifacts": ["Between the memory of", "liminal space", "memory reconsolidation", "hippocampus and prefrontal cortex", "I didn't write this book", "Total words:"], "Zero remaining": lambda content: all(p not in content for p in ( "Between the memory of", "liminal space", "memory reconsolidation", "hippocampus and prefrontal cortex", "I didn't write this book")) } def verify_clean(content): remaining = [] for pattern in verification_checks["AI artifacts"]: if pattern in content: remaining.append(pattern) if remaining: # Calculate line numbers and remove each for pattern in remaining: count = content.count(pattern) print(f" ❌ '{pattern}' found {count} times — removing...") return len(remaining) == 0 ``` **Post-restructuring checks:** - ✅ All chapter headers are sequential (no gaps, no duplicates) - ✅ No duplicate stories appear across multiple chapters - ✅ Placeholder markers like "xx" or "TBD" or "..." are resolved - ✅ Chapter title format is consistent (all "Chapter N:" or all "Chapter N — Title") - ✅ Narrative voice is consistent within each chapter (no first/third-person switching) - ✅ Part/PART headers are sequential and non-duplicated - ✅ The Transition bridge sections are present and connect chapters - ✅ Total word count is within expected range after compression ## Editorial Proposal-Driven Chapter Compression (Memoir/Non-Fiction) ## Editorial Proposal-Driven Chapter Expansion with Scene Work (Memoir/Non-Fiction) When the user provides a list of specific editorial improvement proposals and asks you to rewrite a chapter by EXPANDING specific sections with scene work, sensory detail, and dialogue while preserving other sections intact. ### When to Use This Sub-Skill - User provides a numbered list of editorial improvement proposals calling for **expansion** (e.g., "expand with scene work", "add sensory detail", "show not tell", "add connective tissue", "preserve section X intact") - The chapter needs to grow from a shorter to longer word count (e.g., ~2,289 → ~2,600-2,800 words) - Specific sections need to be **shown** as scenes rather than **summarized** as descriptions - Some sections must be preserved word-for-word while others are expanded - The task involves rewriting a memoir/creative non-fiction chapter, not fiction ### Workflow Steps #### Step 0: Categorize the Editorial Proposals Group each proposal into one of four action categories: | Category | Example | Action | |----------|---------|--------| | **Preserve** | "Keep London section intact" | Do not modify these sections at all — preserve prose, voice, structure | | **Expand with scene work** | "Show Nancy with dialogue, not describe" | Transform summary into scene with dialogue, sensory detail, specific moment | | **Expand with sensory depth** | "Add 2-3 sentences of connective depth to Fermilab" | Layer in specific sensory detail (smells, sounds, physical sensations) | | **Add vignette moments** | "Add 2-3 specific vignette moments" | Create small standalone scenes with dialogue, setting, emotional beat | | **Connective tissue** | "Add transitions between sections" | Write bridge sentences/paragraphs connecting disparate sections | #### Step 1: Identify Preserve-Zone Sections Before rewriting, tag each section with its treatment: - **🔒 PRESERVE** — Do not touch beyond minor grammar fixes - **🔨 EXPAND** — Add scene work, sensory detail, dialogue - **🌉 CONNECT** — Need bridge transitions to/from adjacent sections Read the original chapter and mark which sections fall into each bucket. Block out the preserve sections mentally and never modify them during the rewrite. #### Step 2: Transform Summary into Scene (Show, Don't Tell) For sections marked for expansion with scene work: **Before (summary):** > Bob met Nancy in a grocery store when he was visiting his company's HQ in Michigan. She was standing near the eggs. Bob and Nancy talked for a few minutes and then went their separate ways. **After (scene with dialogue):** > I met Nancy in a grocery store in Michigan, on one of those trips home between flight test rotations. I was standing near the eggs — I remember that detail with absurd clarity, the way you remember the trivial things that frame the moments that change your life — when I noticed the woman next to me, studying the price tag with an expression of genuine outrage. > "Can you believe these prices?" I said, because I had to say something. "Eggs are up, what, a hundred percent?" > She looked at me. Not the quick glance of polite dismissal, but a real look, appraising and amused. "You're not from here," she said. > "How can you tell?" > "The eggs," she said, deadpan. "Only an out-of-towner starts a conversation about eggs." **Key transformation rules:** - Give the character **dialogue** that reveals personality (wit, warmth, intelligence) - Add a **specific physical detail** about the setting (the dairy aisle, the price tag, the expression) - Create a **moment of recognition** — something that signals "this is different" - Use the pause/beat structure of real conversation #### Step 3: Layer in Sensory Depth For sections marked for expansion with sensory depth, add 2-5 sentences that engage the senses: - **Smell**: ozone and solder in a control room, hydraulic fluid in a cockpit, disinfectant in a hospital - **Sound**: the hum of cooling fans, the thud of a canopy sealing, the click of electronics - **Touch**: vibration through a seat, the tightness of a cockpit, the cold of a server room - **Sight**: green text on monitors, cornfields outside a lab window, leaves in autumn - **Emotional weight**: the sacred feeling of being part of something larger, the hollow satisfaction of handoff Each sensory detail should serve a narrative purpose — revealing something about the character's emotional state or the importance of the moment. #### Step 4: Add Specific Vignette Moments For sections marked for vignettes, write 2-4 standalone scenelets that: 1. **Anchor in a specific time/place**: "We were walking through a park near her apartment, late autumn, leaves piled gold and red along the path." 2. **Include a line of dialogue that reveals character**: "A house. A husband. A writing desk by a window. But the house and the husband were the wrong ones. The desk was the only part I got right." 3. **End with an emotional beat**: the moment of knowing, the shift in feeling, the recognition 4. **Advance the relationship**: each vignette should show the connection deepening Good vignette placement: the moment they met, the moment they first had a real conversation, the moment he knew, the night before a separation, a specific shared experience. #### Step 5: Write Connective Tissue Between Sections Between sections that were originally abrupt, write bridge sentences/paragraphs that: - **Contrast** the previous and next environments: "The transition was jarring. At Fermilab, the culture was academic — professorial, collaborative, unhurried. At Eglin, everything moved at the speed of jet exhaust." - **Show the character's emotional state** at the transition point: "When the final handoff came, I felt a hollow satisfaction. The system worked beautifully. But it belonged to someone else now." - **Use a physical action** to mark the transition: "I packed my desk, walked past the cornfields one last time, and drove away wondering what came next." Avoid generic transition phrases like "meanwhile," "later," "after that." Use specific imagery from the setting being left behind. #### Step 6: Preserve Voice Consistency When expanding sections, maintain consistent narrative voice: - For a **first-person memoir**: all new expansion must be in first-person (I, my, me) — but leave quoted dialogue in the speaker's natural voice - For a **third-person biography**: stay in third-person - The preserved sections set the voice — match it exactly in all new material - No "lecture voice" in expansions: avoid "As I reflect on this now..." or academic framing #### Step 7: Hit the Expansion Word Count Target Write the full rewrite in one pass, then check word count: - If **under target**: Add more sensory detail to the thinnest section, or add another vignette moment - If **over target**: Tighten connective tissue and vignette descriptions without removing the scene-dialogue-emotional beat structure Target within ~50 words of the requested range. Favor landing closer to the top of the range when expanding (the goal is richness, not tightness). #### Step 8: End-of-Rewrite Verification Run this checklist before delivering: - [ ] Preserve-zone sections are verbatim (aside from minor grammar/consistency fixes) - [ ] Expanded sections have dialogue + sensory detail + emotional beat - [ ] Vignette moments are specific (time, place, dialogue, feeling) - [ ] Connective tissue bridges abrupt section transitions - [ ] Word count is within target range - [ ] Voice is consistent throughout (no drift between old and new material) - [ ] All original facts preserved (dates, names, locations unchanged) - [ ] No AI lecture-voice introduced in expansions - [ ] Grammar fixes applied throughout (no "returned back", "could of", double words, etc.) ### Expansion Patterns Reference | Summary → Scene | |----------------| | "Bob met Nancy in a grocery store" → scene with dialogue about eggs, her deadpan humor, the laughter, the moment of connection | | "They talked and went their separate ways" → "I spent the next three days kicking myself for not asking for her number" | | "He learned the systems intimately" → "I spent my days in a windowless control room, surrounded by racks of electronics that hummed and clicked like living things. The air smelled of ozone and solder." | | Thin Description → Sensory Depth | |-----------------------------------| | "He worked on avionics integration" → "The cockpit was tight, switches and dials packed so densely it felt like sitting inside a circuit diagram. The canopy sealed shut with a thud that cut off the outside world." | | No Transition → Connective Tissue | |------------------------------------| | "The job ended." → "When the final handoff came, I felt a hollow satisfaction. The system worked beautifully. But it belonged to someone else now. I packed my desk, walked past the cornfields one last time, and drove away wondering what came next." | ### Common Pitfalls | Pitfall | Solution | |---------|----------| | Accidentally modifying preserve sections | Block them out mentally. After writing, diff against original to confirm preserves. | | Adding dialogue that doesn't match the character's voice | Base dialogue on any existing dialogue in the preserved sections for tone. | | Expanding without adding emotional weight | Each expansion should do double duty: add detail AND reveal character/emotion. | | Breaking narrative voice between new and old material | Read the entire chapter aloud after writing — voice breaks are audible. | | Losing track of the word count target during expansion | Write generously first, then trim to fit. | | Introducing new facts not in the original | Never add new biographical details.
